stories.title: The Weight of Unread Pages
stories.excerpt: A woman inherits her grandmother's library and finds a note in every book that was never finished.
stories.body:
Her grandmother's library took up an entire wall of the sunroom, floor to ceiling, organized by a system no one else had ever cracked. When the lawyer handed over the keys, he mentioned the books almost as an afterthought — as if a thousand spines were a minor inconvenience compared to the house itself.

She found the first note on a Tuesday, tucked into a copy of a novel she'd never heard of. Just a scrap of paper, her grandmother's handwriting gone soft with age: Made it to page 140. Couldn't finish. Too much like my mother.

The second note was in a mystery, dog-eared at the halfway point. Knew who did it. Didn't want to be right. The third was folded into a cookbook, of all things, wedged between a recipe for bread and a recipe for something in French she couldn't translate. Never made this. Ran out of time, not flour.

By the twentieth note, she'd stopped reading the books themselves and started reading only the notes, moving down the shelf like she was excavating a person one abandoned page at a time. Some books had no notes at all — the finished ones, she assumed, the ones that hadn't asked anything of her grandmother she wasn't ready to give.

She found the last note in the very last book, on the bottom shelf, in a paperback so worn the cover had softened to felt. It wasn't a comment on the story. It didn't reference a page number. It just said: If you're reading this, you finished cleaning out the shelf, which means you finally forgave me for never finishing anything. I'm sorry it took a library to say it.

She sat on the floor of the sunroom for a long time after that, surrounded by a thousand unfinished stories, and understood, finally, that her grandmother hadn't failed to finish them. She'd simply decided, book by book, exactly how much of each ending she was willing to carry. And now, so would she.

stories.title: Letters to No One in Particular
stories.excerpt: A retired postman starts writing letters to the addresses on his old route, just to keep his handwriting from disappearing.
stories.body:
Frank had walked the same six streets for thirty-one years, and in his first month of retirement he realized he missed the houses more than the job. Not the people, particularly — he'd barely spoken to most of them beyond a nod at the gate. He missed knowing what was behind each door.

So he started writing letters. Not to anyone he knew — to the addresses themselves, the way he used to know them. Dear 14 Marlow Street, he wrote, I hope the dog is still getting out for its walks now that the ice has thawed. Dear 9 Farrow Lane, the maple out front must be enormous by now.

He never sent them. He kept them in a drawer, dated, filed by street, the closest thing he had to a diary. His handwriting, which had gone loose and impatient over three decades of junk mail and bills, slowly tightened back into the careful cursive his mother had taught him, letter by letter, evening by evening.

It was his daughter who found the drawer, eventually, looking for tape. She read four letters before she understood what she was holding, and didn't tell him she'd found them for another two years — not because she was hiding it, but because she wasn't sure yet what it would mean to say it out loud.

When she finally did, she asked him why he never sent any of them. Frank thought about it for a long moment. Because they were never really letters, he said. They were just me, checking that I still knew how to pay attention to something. The dog didn't need to hear it. I did.

stories.title: The Last Page First
stories.excerpt: A boy who always reads endings before beginnings meets a librarian who refuses to tell him how her own story ends.
stories.body:
Every book Theo ever loved, he ruined on purpose. He'd crack the spine, flip to the last page, read the final line, and only then go back to the beginning — armored, he thought, against disappointment.

The librarian caught him doing it to a battered copy of a novel with a blue cover, and instead of scolding him, she just asked why. He told her: so nothing can surprise me. She considered this for a moment and said that was a very sad way to read a book, and an even sadder way to live a life.

He asked her, then, how her own story ended. She smiled the way adults do when they've decided not to lie to a child but also not to tell them everything. I don't know yet, she said. That's rather the point of still being in it.

Theo thought about that for the rest of the summer. In September, he opened a new book, one with a cracked yellow cover, and for the first time in years, he started on page one and did not look ahead. He was terrified the whole way through. He finished it anyway.
